course.title: Django Full-Stack Web Development

lessons.body:
Django Setup & MTV Pattern

Django is a Python web framework for building full web apps quickly. Install it with pip install django, then create a project with django-admin startproject mysite. A project is the whole website; inside it you build apps — one app per feature, such as a blog app or a shop app — with python manage.py startapp blog. The manage.py script is your command centre for running the server, making migrations and more.

Django follows the MTV pattern: Model, Template, View. The Model is the data layer — Python classes that map to database tables. The Template is the presentation layer — HTML with placeholders for data. The View is the logic in the middle: it receives the web request, talks to the model, and picks a template to render. MTV is Django's version of the older MVC idea, with the view playing the controller's role. URLs glue it together: urls.py maps each web address to a view function.

pip install django
django-admin startproject mysite
cd mysite
python manage.py startapp blog
python manage.py runserver
# Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in the browser

Step by step: install Django, scaffold the project, add an app for your feature, then run the built-in development server and open the address it prints.

  • Key points
  • A Django project holds the whole site; an app holds one feature.
  • MTV means Model (data), Template (HTML) and View (logic).
  • urls.py maps each URL to a view; manage.py runserver starts the dev server on port 8000.

mcqs.q: Which command creates a new Django project?
mcqs.why: django-admin startproject scaffolds a new Django project with settings, urls.py and manage.py.

mcqs.q: What does MTV stand for in Django?
mcqs.why: MTV is Django's architecture: the Model holds data, the Template renders HTML, and the View holds the logic.

mcqs.q: Which file maps a URL to a view function?
mcqs.why: urls.py holds the URL patterns; each pattern points an address at the view that should handle it.

mcqs.q: Which command starts Django's development server?
mcqs.why: runserver starts the built-in development server, by default at http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

mcqs.q: In the MTV pattern, which part talks to the database?
mcqs.why: The Model defines the data as Python classes that Django maps to database tables.

tasks.answer: startproject is the django-admin subcommand that scaffolds a new Django project.
tasks.hint: Which subcommand scaffolds a brand-new project?

lessons.body:
Models & ORM

A Django model is a Python class that describes one database table. Each attribute is a field: title = models.CharField(max_length=200) becomes a text column, price = models.IntegerField() a number column. Every model inherits from models.Model and gets an automatic id primary key.

You never write SQL by hand for everyday work — Django's ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) translates Python into SQL. After changing a model, run python manage.py makemigrations to generate a migration file describing the change, then python manage.py migrate to apply it to the database. Query with the model's manager: Book.objects.all() returns every book, Book.objects.filter(author="Sid") returns matching ones, and Book.objects.get(id=1) returns exactly one. Queries return QuerySets, which are lazy — the database is only hit when you actually use the results.

from django.db import models

class Book(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    author = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    price = models.IntegerField()

# python manage.py makemigrations
# python manage.py migrate
Book.objects.create(title="Django Basics", author="Sid", price=499)
cheap = Book.objects.filter(price__lt=500)  # QuerySet of books under 500

Step by step: define the model class, make and apply the migration, then create and query rows through the ORM instead of raw SQL.

  • Key points
  • Models inherit from models.Model; each field maps to a database column.
  • makemigrations creates the migration; migrate applies it.
  • objects.filter() returns a lazy QuerySet; get() returns a single object.

mcqs.q: Which class must every Django model inherit from?
mcqs.why: Inheriting from models.Model gives the class Django's ORM behaviour: table mapping, managers and migrations.

mcqs.q: Which command generates migration files after you change a model?
mcqs.why: makemigrations inspects the models and writes a migration file describing the change; migrate is the command that applies it.

mcqs.q: Which command applies pending migrations to the database?
mcqs.why: migrate runs the pending migration files against the database, creating or altering tables.

options: A QuerySet of all books by Sid
mcqs.q: What does Book.objects.filter(author="Sid") return?
mcqs.why: filter() returns a QuerySet — a lazy collection of the matching rows, which may hold zero, one or many books.

mcqs.q: Which field type stores short text with a maximum length?
mcqs.why: CharField stores short strings and requires max_length; TextField is for long unbounded text.

tasks.answer: CharField requires a max_length argument, because the database column needs a known size; without it Django raises an error at startup.
tasks.hint: Which field is missing a required argument, and what does the database need to know about a text column?
tasks.prompt: This model crashes when Django loads it. What is wrong and what is the fix?
tasks.title: Fix the bug

lessons.body:
Views, Templates & Forms

A view is a Python function that takes a request and returns a response. The simplest view returns HttpResponse("Hello"); in practice you use render(request, "blog/home.html", {"name": "Sid"}), which loads a template, fills it with the context dictionary, and returns the finished HTML.

Templates are HTML with two kinds of markup: variables in double braces — {{ name }} prints the value — and tags in brace-percent — {% for book in books %}...{% endfor %} loops, {% if user %}...{% endif %} branches. Templates can extend a base layout with {% extends "base.html" %} and fill its blocks, so every page shares one header and footer.

Forms collect user input. A ModelForm builds a form automatically from a model, and in the template you render it with {{ form.as_p }} plus {% csrf_token %}, which inserts a hidden token that protects the form against Cross-Site Request Forgery. In the view, form.is_valid() checks the submitted data and form.save() writes it to the database.

# views.py
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):
    return render(request, "blog/home.html", {"name": "Sid"})

# blog/home.html
# <h1>Hello {{ name }}!</h1>
# renders as: <h1>Hello Sid!</h1>

Step by step: the view builds a context dictionary, render() merges it into the template, and the browser receives plain HTML with the values filled in.

  • Key points
  • A view takes a request and returns a response, usually via render().
  • {{ variable }} prints a value; {% tag %} adds logic such as loops and ifs.
  • ModelForm builds a form from a model; always include {% csrf_token %}.

options: An HttpResponse object (such as the result of render())
mcqs.q: What must a Django view function return?
mcqs.why: Django expects a view to return an HttpResponse; render() builds one from a template and context.

mcqs.q: How do you print a variable's value inside a Django template?
mcqs.why: Double braces mark a template variable, so {{ name }} is replaced by the value from the context.

mcqs.q: Which template tag loops over a list?
mcqs.why: The for tag iterates over a list and endfor closes the block; anything between them repeats per item.

mcqs.q: What does {% csrf_token %} protect a form against?
mcqs.why: The CSRF token proves the form submission came from your own site, so another site cannot trick a logged-in user into submitting it.

options: A form that only works with HTML tables
A form class automatically generated from a model, with fields and validation
A template for the admin site
mcqs.q: What is a ModelForm?
mcqs.why: ModelForm reads a model's fields and builds a matching form, so form.save() can write straight to the database.

tasks.answer:
render() replaces {{ name }} with the context value "Sid", so the template produces

Hello Sid!

.
tasks.hint: What value does {{ name }} take from the context dictionary?
tasks.prompt: The view passes {"name": "Sid"} to this template. What HTML does the browser receive?
tasks.title: Predict the output

lessons.body:
User Authentication

Django ships with a complete auth system in django.contrib.auth: a built-in User model, login/logout views, password hashing and sessions. Passwords are never stored in plain text — Django hashes them with PBKDF2, so even someone reading the database cannot recover the original password.

To log a user in, check the credentials with authenticate(request, username=..., password=...), which returns the user or None, then call login(request, user) to start a session. logout(request) ends it. To protect a view, add the @login_required decorator above it — anonymous visitors are redirected to the login page instead. For sign-up, the built-in UserCreationForm handles username and password validation for you.

from django.contrib.auth import authenticate, login, logout
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required

def signin(request):
    user = authenticate(request, username="sid", password="secret123")
    if user is not None:
        login(request, user)  # starts a session
        return redirect("home")
    return render(request, "login.html", {"error": "Wrong credentials"})

@login_required
def dashboard(request):
    return render(request, "dashboard.html")

Step by step: authenticate() verifies the password hash, login() creates the session cookie, and @login_required guards any view that only signed-in users may see.

  • Key points
  • authenticate() checks credentials and returns the user or None.
  • login() starts a session; logout() ends it.
  • @login_required redirects anonymous visitors to the login page.

mcqs.q: Which function checks a username and password against the database?
mcqs.why: authenticate() compares the given credentials with the stored (hashed) password and returns the user, or None if they do not match.

mcqs.q: Which decorator forces a visitor to be logged in before seeing a view?
mcqs.why: @login_required from django.contrib.auth.decorators redirects anonymous users to the login page.

options: Hashed with PBKDF2, never in plain text
mcqs.q: How does Django store user passwords?
mcqs.why: Django hashes passwords with PBKDF2, so the original password cannot be recovered from the database.

options: It starts a session for the user in the current request
It creates a new user account
mcqs.q: What does login(request, user) do?
mcqs.why: login() attaches the authenticated user to the session, so later requests know who is signed in.

mcqs.q: Which built-in form creates a new user account with password validation?
mcqs.why: UserCreationForm is Django's built-in sign-up form: it validates the username and the two password fields.

tasks.answer: @login_required guards the view: anonymous visitors are redirected to the login page instead of seeing the dashboard.
tasks.hint: Which decorator from django.contrib.auth.decorators requires a signed-in user?
tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing decorator so only logged-in users can open the dashboard view.

lessons.body:
REST APIs with DRF

A REST API lets other programs — a mobile app, a React frontend, another server — use your Django data over HTTP. Django REST Framework (DRF) adds this on top of Django. Its core piece is the serializer: a class that converts a model instance into JSON for the response, and converts incoming JSON back into validated data.

Views become API views: APIView has a get() method for reads and a post() method for creates, or you can use generic views such as ListCreateAPIView and RetrieveUpdateDestroyAPIView which handle the common cases in a few lines. A ModelViewSet bundles all CRUD operations for a model, and a router maps it to URLs automatically — router.register("books", BookViewSet) creates list, detail, create, update and delete endpoints in one line. Status codes matter: 200 means OK, 201 means a resource was created, 400 means bad input, 404 means not found.

from rest_framework import serializers, viewsets, routers
from .models import Book

class BookSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Book
        fields = "__all__"

class BookViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Book.objects.all()
    serializer_class = BookSerializer

router = routers.DefaultRouter()
router.register("books", BookViewSet)
# GET  /books/     -> list all books (200)
# POST /books/     -> create a book (201)

Step by step: the serializer defines the JSON shape, the ViewSet provides the CRUD logic, and the router wires the URLs — no template is involved at all.

  • Key points
  • A serializer converts model instances to JSON and validates incoming JSON.
  • ModelViewSet gives full CRUD; a router creates its URLs automatically.
  • Use the right status code: 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 bad input, 404 not found.

options: It converts model instances to JSON and validates incoming JSON
mcqs.q: What does a DRF serializer do?
mcqs.why: Serializers translate between Django model instances and JSON, the format APIs send over HTTP.

mcqs.q: Which DRF class gives you full CRUD (list, create, retrieve, update, delete) for a model in one class?
mcqs.why: ModelViewSet bundles all five CRUD actions for a model; combined with a router it needs almost no extra code.

mcqs.q: Which HTTP status code means a resource was successfully created?
mcqs.why: 201 Created is the standard response for a successful POST that creates a new resource; 200 is for a plain successful request.

options: It automatically maps the ViewSet to list/detail/create/update/delete URLs
mcqs.q: What does router.register("books", BookViewSet) do?
mcqs.why: A DRF router generates the URL patterns for a ViewSet, so one line creates all five CRUD endpoints.

mcqs.q: In an APIView, which method handles a GET request?
mcqs.why: APIView dispatches by HTTP method: a GET request calls the view's get() method, POST calls post().

tasks.answer: A ModelSerializer's Meta must declare fields (or exclude); without it DRF raises an error because it does not know which model fields to include in the JSON.
tasks.hint: What does Meta need to tell the serializer about which model fields to expose?
tasks.prompt: This serializer crashes with an error about fields. What is missing and what is the fix?
tasks.title: Fix the bug

lessons.body:
Deploy to Production

Running Django on your laptop is development; production is a real server that strangers visit. Three settings must change before you deploy. First, set DEBUG = False — with debug on, Django shows detailed error pages that leak your code and settings to anyone who triggers an error. Second, set ALLOWED_HOSTS to the domain names your site answers on, such as ["mysite.pythonanywhere.com"]; Django refuses requests for any other host. Third, move SECRET_KEY out of the code into an environment variable — anyone who has it can forge signed cookies and sessions.

Then prepare the app: run python manage.py collectstatic to gather all CSS, JavaScript and images into one folder the web server can serve, and run migrations on the server database. A production server such as Gunicorn runs your Django code (Django's runserver is for development only), behind a web server or a platform such as PythonAnywhere. Deploy in small steps and check the live site after each one.

# settings.py (production)
DEBUG = False
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["mysite.pythonanywhere.com"]
SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY")

# on the server
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py collectstatic
# run with gunicorn, never with runserver

Step by step: turn debug off, allow only your real host, move the secret key into the environment, collect static files, migrate, and serve with Gunicorn.

  • Key points
  • DEBUG = False in production — debug pages leak internals.
  • ALLOWED_HOSTS lists the domains the site may answer for.
  • collectstatic gathers static files; Gunicorn serves the app, not runserver.

mcqs.q: What must DEBUG be set to in production?
mcqs.why: With DEBUG = True, Django shows detailed error pages that expose code, paths and settings to anyone who triggers an error.

mcqs.q: Which setting lists the hostnames your Django site is allowed to answer for?
mcqs.why: ALLOWED_HOSTS is Django's host-header check: requests for hosts not on the list are rejected.

mcqs.q: Which command gathers all static files into one folder for the production server?
mcqs.why: collectstatic copies every app's CSS, JavaScript and images into STATIC_ROOT so the web server can serve them.

options: It makes the site load faster
Anyone with it can forge signed cookies and sessions
It is too long to type
Django refuses to start with a key in code
mcqs.q: Why must SECRET_KEY be kept out of your code and put in an environment variable?
mcqs.why: SECRET_KEY signs sessions and tokens; leaking it lets an attacker forge a session and act as any user.

mcqs.q: Which server should run Django in production?
mcqs.why: runserver is a single-threaded development server; Gunicorn is a production WSGI server built to handle real traffic.

tasks.answer: DEBUG must be False in production, otherwise Django shows detailed error pages that leak code and settings.
tasks.hint: Should debug mode be on or off on a live site?
tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing value so this production settings file is safe.
